questions.context: Canon already lets magic cut across consent: a Sacrament anchor holds 'regardless of whether the anchor consents' (R29-1), and Obsession Force (the Fracture of Worlds law of possessive fixation) steered a queen into marriage in the Kujo arc. Your fair-play line wants every ability to carry a tell and a counter a player can find.

options.label: Compliance, never desire
options.consequence: Pressure, a Draft or a working can bend a body to stillness or compliance, but desire stays the person's own; any scene under one is dubcon or non-con by definition.

options.label: Desire, with tell and counter
options.consequence: An Obsession or Attraction working, a charm or a Draft may make someone want; it shows a tell, has a findable counter, costs its user, and the aftermath knows it was made.

options.label: Barred from the bed
options.consequence: No working, Draft or Pressure touches desire or consent; magic stays out of intimacy entirely.

questions.rec_reason: Canon has already done it (the Kujo arc, R29-1), and B holds it to the fairness every other ability meets: a tell, a counter, a cost and a reckoning after.

questions.title: The body under coercion
questions.question: In a dubcon or non-con scene, may the victim's body respond with arousal on the page, and how is it framed?
questions.context: Rule 9 writes dubcon and non-con (no consent at all) 'with the same specificity'. Arousal non-concordance (genital response and felt desire running apart; Chivers, Nagoski) and tonic immobility (freezing under threat) are real, and the old bodice-ripper used that response as proof of wanting. The narrator never adjudicates (R5-E).

options.label: Fear only
options.consequence: Under coercion the body shows fear and shutdown only (freezing, nausea, a held object); no arousal is written.
options.sample: Hrefna split rounds until the light went, because the stack was low and the axe asked nothing of her. Twice she stood with the blade raised and could not bring it down. The night came back in pieces: his weight, her arms gone to lead, the blubber lamp guttering on the shelf and her eyes fixed on it, counting its spits, while the rest of her went far away and cold.

options.label: Shown, known as reflex
options.consequence: Arousal may be written, and the POV knows it for the body's reflex, apart from her will; she carries that knowledge into the aftermath.
options.sample: Hrefna split rounds until the light went, because the stack was low and the axe asked nothing of her. Twice she stood with the blade raised and could not bring it down. The night came back in pieces: his weight, her arms gone to lead, and her own cunt gone slick under him as if it belonged to some other woman. She knew what that was. A struck knee kicks. Wet wood, her mother would have said of a liar, and her body had lied.

options.label: Shown, left unread
options.consequence: Arousal may be written and nobody names what it means; the reader decides, and the ambiguity is the scene's weight.
options.sample: Hrefna split rounds until the light went, because the stack was low and the axe asked nothing of her. Twice she stood with the blade raised and could not bring it down. The night came back in pieces: his weight, her arms gone to lead, and her own cunt gone slick under him. She split another round. At the door her neighbour asked how her stack was, and she said full, and went in to sit by the night-stone with her back to the wall.

questions.rec_reason: It writes the truth of the body at Rule 9's specificity while keeping the bodice-ripper's lie out, and the knowledge is the aftermath's sharpest edge.

questions.title: Carrying it forward
questions.question: After a non-con or coerced scene, how does it carry into later scenes?
questions.context: Rule 9 never skips the aftermath, and R70-115 lets restraint break 'at a small, unexpected thing'. Judith Herman's Trauma and Recovery (1992) maps recovery as safety, remembrance, then reconnection. Much dark fiction drops the matter after a chapter; grimdark sends a bill to the world: feud, pregnancy, scandal, blood-debt.

options.label: In the body and habit
options.consequence: The survivor's later scenes carry it physically (the startle, sleep that will not come, the seat with its back to the wall) until the thread resolves it.

options.label: The bill reaches the world
options.consequence: The act opens or advances a Front: feud, blood-debt, pregnancy, scandal or a case at law; the perpetrator's own account is a lie in his mouth (Rule 8).

options.label: Recovery logged in stages
options.consequence: The Ledger tracks where the survivor stands (safe, remembering, reconnecting) so each scene knows what she can bear; the stages are never named on the page.

questions.rec_reason: Both are WOTR's own method, cost in the body and a bill in the world; C's stages are a therapist's map and would make the Ledger read like a case file.

questions.title: The aftermath beat
questions.question: What shape does the aftermath of an explicit scene take on the page?
questions.context: Rule 9: 'aftermath never skipped'. For fights you chose 'procedure as craft' (R71-21), and R2-5 rules that after a Single Act nobody says what it meant; the change shows 'in how they handle the bucket'. The archive's best aftermaths are care for small things: a coat mended, a pulse counted again.

options.label: Procedure, meaning unsaid
options.consequence: The aftermath is the small work after (washing, the fire fed, clothes found, the door), and neither partner says what it meant; the change shows in how they do it.
options.sample: Afterward Hrefna got up first. She wiped herself with a rag from the shelf, pulled her shirt down and fed the blubber lamp from the jar, and when it caught she held her hands to it. Bjarki lay on the hides and watched her. She found his belt where she had thrown it, coiled it, and set it by his boots. Then she went out into the cold and brought in an armful from the woodpile, and stacked it at the hearth, three more rounds than the night needed.

options.label: Pillow talk, truths traded
options.consequence: The aftermath is the one time guarded people talk: secrets, plans, a confession, and what is said goes on the Ledger (K6).
options.sample: Afterward they lay in the hides with the lamp low and her head on his arm, and Bjarki told her about the winter he had eaten his own horse on the Ridgewall, which he had told nobody. Hrefna listened. When he was done she told him where her husband's silver lay buried, under the night-stone, and that the headman's son had asked her twice. Bjarki said nothing to that. He drew the hide over her shoulder and kept his hand there.

options.label: By the pair
options.consequence: Each pair's card names its shape, procedure or talk, and the aftermath keeps to it; a change of shape is itself a beat.
options.sample: They always talked after, these two; it was the part Hrefna liked best. Tonight Bjarki got up as soon as he had come, wiped himself on his shirt-tail and went out to the woodpile in his bare feet. She heard the axe. She lay in the hides and counted the strokes, and when he came back with an armful and stacked it at the hearth without looking at her, she knew he had said yes to the headman's road.

questions.rec_reason: It is your fight aftermath and the archive's own strongest note, love as maintenance, and R2-5's silence makes every later scene carry the change.

questions.title: Your character in the bed
questions.question: In a roleplay turn, what may Natalie write of your character's body during an explicit scene?
questions.context: Natalie never thinks, speaks or acts for your PC (R49-01, R52-10). For fights you ruled 'wounds as world facts', with 'how he bears it' yours (R71-6). Yoko Mishiro, his canon wife, is an NPC Natalie voices, so the bed needs the same line drawn before it is needed.

options.label: His post, her answer
options.consequence: Natalie writes only the partner and the room; every act of his body, and every response in it, comes from your post, and the turn stops wherever his body would next move.

options.label: Contact as world fact
options.consequence: Once your post sets the act, contact, position and what the partner does to him are world facts; his arousal, pleasure, pain and climax, and how he bears them, stay yours.

questions.rec_reason: It is your fight ruling moved to the bed, so the scene runs as a scene instead of halting at every touch, while everything he feels stays in your hands.

questions.title: The explicit roleplay turn
questions.question: How does a full roleplay turn run when the scene in it is explicit?
questions.context: Every reply is a full turn of about 3,500 words (R49-30), and every turn stops at your next decision (Table Rule 1); in bed the decisions come fast. For fights you allowed standing orders, conditions Natalie runs 'until the first branch they do not cover' (R71-5).

options.label: Partner and world fill it
options.consequence: The turn runs on the partner's side and the world beyond the door (the house, the watch, the weather) up to his next decision, half texture and talk, half the world moving (R49-29).

options.label: Standing orders in bed
options.consequence: You may post the course of the encounter, a pace, a limit or a stop for your character, and Natalie runs it to the first branch it does not cover, then stops there.

options.label: Short turns in bed
options.consequence: This reopens R49-30: an explicit turn may run short and stop at each decision, so the exchange moves at the speed of the act.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps your full-length turn and your character in your hands at once, the same answer you gave for fights; A's world beyond the door still fills what the orders leave.

questions.title: An NPC who would force him
questions.question: If an NPC would coerce or force your character, how far does the turn go?
questions.context: NPCs pursue their wants (Table Rule 3), and some will want to take what is not offered. In a fight an NPC's blow lands as world fact once your move resolves (R71-6). Coercion of a player's own character is where tables most need a clear line, and it covers guest players at the Discord table too.

options.label: Lands like a blow
options.consequence: The NPC's act is written as a world fact, as a wound would be; how he bears it is yours.

options.label: Threat placed, his post decides
options.consequence: Natalie sets the threat in the room (the grip, the bargain, the Draft in the cup) and stops; the act reaches the page only through your post.

options.label: Never against a PC
options.consequence: NPCs may want it and say so; no NPC forces or coerces a player's character on the page.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps Rule 3's dangerous NPC and Rule 1's stop at your decision together, and gives a guest player at the Discord table the same say you have.

questions.title: Checks for explicit scenes
questions.question: Which checks should verify_scene run on an explicit scene?
questions.context: verify_scene has no explicit mode. Its firearms list counts 'cock' as gun vocabulary, and nothing checks Rule 9's clauses or the floor. The style and combat laws each added checks by vote (R70-136, R71-103).

options.label: Rule 9 checklist
options.consequence: An --explicit flag WARNs when a scene lacks a position fix, a scent, a sound or mimetic word, or an aftermath beat after the act.

options.label: The floor check
options.consequence: FAIL when an explicit scene names anyone whose card or roster row gives an age under eighteen, or no age at all; the body's age counts, never a soul's.

options.label: Collision fixes
options.consequence: Under --explicit the firearms list ignores anatomical 'cock', and 'aftercare' and 'safeword' are flagged in narration only.

options.label: Bed stock-phrase bans
options.consequence: Romance stock joins the hard-ban list in narration: euphemisms that dodge R49-51 (her sex, his member, her core, mewled) and stock bed cliches.

questions.rec_reason: B makes the floor mechanical instead of a matter of memory, and the rest hold each scene to Rule 9 and R49-51 the way the combat checks hold a fight.

settled.point: The floor: adults only, nothing sexual involving minors ever, no explicit sex on real living people, no bestiality. Adult beastkin are people; beasts, Well-spawn and summons are not.
settled.why_not_asked: NATALIE.md's floor is fixed and never on a questionnaire; it is not a rule row. Every sample here is between adults.

settled.point: Table Rule 9's clauses: plain anatomical vocabulary, clinical specificity, positions tracked, arousal scents, onomatopoeia, the NPC's own desire and refusal line and change of mind, a consequence, dubcon and non-con at the same specificity, aftermath never skipped.
settled.why_not_asked: Standing law in NATALIE.md, extended by XS1 and XS2; SC3, K5 and SC13 ask only how its clauses are carried out.

settled.point: Explicit narration is plain and crude: working-man anatomical words, lush in sensation, blunt in naming.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-26 and kept by the style law; SC1 asks only whose words.

settled.point: Season imagery, the held detail at the peak, the poem after, and mimetic words romanised and never italic, all beside the plain words.
The techniques are keyed to the POV's culture; the lover's culture shows in what they do and say.
Isaac's PC and the other creators' characters are never thought, voiced or acted for; Isaac may voice any NPC, a lover included.
settled.why_not_asked: Standing law; SC14 to SC16 ask only where the line falls in bed.

settled.point: NPC thought: one italic thought per NPC in a roleplay turn, none under a written scene's POV lock, so a partner's desire shows through body and speech there.
Third person only; roleplay turns in present tense, written scenes in past.
The narrator never passes a moral verdict on what happens in bed; a verdict lives only in the POV's own idiom.
settled.why_not_asked: Standing anti-machine law; SC11 builds on it.

settled.point: Pop-psych words (boundaries, triggered, closure) stay out of narration; modern words, safeword and aftercare among them, are legal in speech and italic thought.
settled.why_not_asked: Vocabulary law; SC8 asks only how a game is framed in the world.

settled.point: Profanity in speech and close POV, each culture's own swears first.
Jo-ha-kyū tempo for set pieces and kishōtenketsu (set-up, development, twist, reconciliation) for quiet scenes reach explicit scenes as they reach any other.
settled.why_not_asked: SP1 and SP2; K3 asks only which strand leads the act.

settled.point: Feeling carried by one held image and never named; a scene may close on verse set apart.
A lover gets the full first-sight inventory in the POV's own order, and one changed detail on each return.
settled.why_not_asked: Description law applies to lovers as to anyone.

settled.point: Turns run about 3,500 words and set pieces 5,000 and up.
settled.why_not_asked: Prose law; SC2 and SC15 ask only how explicit scenes use those lengths.

settled.point: Every working costs something visible in the body, and no figure is invented.
settled.why_not_asked: Standing law; SC7 and SC10 build on it.

settled.point: Each culture's own sound and state words, entered in its Inventory and never italic.
settled.why_not_asked: RH4; the bed draws on the same banks.

settled.point: NPCs lie, refuse and pursue their wants, and a betrayal is foreshadowed so a player could catch it.
settled.why_not_asked: Table Rules 3 and 8 and the play law; a lover is an NPC like any other.

settled.point: Medicine is true to place and purse.
settled.why_not_asked: World texture and combat law; K6 asks only what the Ledger keeps.
